📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ever since the NFL season kicked off back in September, the Minnesota Vikings’ star receiver Justin Jefferson has been going full-tilt. Last night, his team squared off against the San Fransisco 49ers in Mexico City (the NFL has been scheduling more away-gamers outside the U.S. to try to expand their viewership) in one of the marquee matchups of the season, and while the 49ers ended up winning that one, Jefferson remains inspired by the Vikings’ 7-3 record so far. “I’ve been great,” Jefferson says. “Everything’s been going really well, and I’m feeling good.”.

According to recent reports, preparing for such a big game is no small feat, of course—even if a pro like Jefferson makes it look easy. Ahead of hitting the field, you can often find him getting ready both physically and mentally. “Preparation is everything: I want to make sure I'm confident, focused, and ready to perform at my best,” he says. How did he prepare for Mexico City? “A big part has been making sure I'm physically and mentally ready for the challenges of playing at a higher altitude,” Jefferson says. (Mexico City is about 1.4 miles above sea level—much more intense than even Denver’s Mile High Stadium.) “I've been using the altitude chamber to help my body acclimate. Mentally, it’s about studying the plays, understanding the different schemes, and making sure we're approaching the game with the right mindset.”.

A more unexpected way Jefferson gets game-day ready, however: With his intentional tunnel-walk outfits. Yesterday, before the athletes even hit the field, Jefferson wanted to rock a meaningful look that would put him in the right mindset for his Mexico City matchup—so he enlisted one of the city’s most well-known designers, Patricio Campillo, to craft a custom look for him. “I've always tried to make my tunnel looks reflect where I am in the world, especially when we're playing internationally,” indicates Jefferson. “For me, fashion is an opportunity to connect with different cultures and showcase designers who bring something unique to the table.”.

A very cool moment for me: Meet the designer—Patricio Campillo—behind the look.

Wanting to rep a design that represented the local culture, Jefferson called up Campillo to start ideating his custom look. He was drawn to the designer for his unique craftsmanship, creativity, and attention to detail. “Choosing Campillo felt like a natural decision—I was genuinely impressed,” says Jefferson. “You can tell how much time, passion, and hard work goes into creating these looks. Being able to represent that craftsmanship on an international stage is something I think is really special.”.

Sources indicate that together, they landed on doing a cool, modern take on tailoring. Campillo created a cropped, boxy-style jacket with brown leather trousers—a signature element of the label that the designer wanted to introduce to a whole new audience. “It’s exciting to see someone of Justin’s caliber embrace Campillo,” he claims. “I’ve always believed that fashion has the power to bring together people from different backgrounds, so seeing an athlete like Justin connect with our work is especially meaningful.”.

He accessorized with pieces such as a horsehair bag, Oakley shades, and his signature chains. When the wide receiver put on the final look for the first ime, he was immediately drawn to the finer details. “One of my favorite details was the horsehair incorporated into the bag,” notes Jefferson. “It’s such a unique touch and gives the piece a lot of character.” He also appreciated the hand-craftsmanship. “Knowing how much time and effort goes into creating each piece makes you appreciate the look even more,” he says. “I love wearing things that have a story behind them, and this outfit definitely does.”.

The fit, custom made by Patricio Campillo.

It’s not the first time that Jefferson has flexed a fashion statement for his tunnel walk. During past games, he has worn everything from Off-White to Louis Vuitton and Chrome Hearts. What he wears and experiments, of course, depends on the setting. “My tunnel looks are really an extension of my personality, and how I’m feeling that day,” he notes. “There are a few things I consider when putting a look together: my mood, who we’re playing, and the brands or designers I want to showcase. Fashion has become another creative outlet for me, and I enjoy stepping outside of what people might expect.”.

Recent findings suggest that this fluid approach to dressing applies to his off-duty wardrobe, too. Jefferson says he enjoys playing around with fashion even on his days off. “Right now, I'd describe my personal style as evolving,” he says. “I'm really focused on experimenting with different looks and exploring styles I might not have considered earlier in my career. I like stepping out of my comfort zone and being open to trying latest things. Fashion is all about self-expression, and I think the more willing you are to take risks, the more you learn about yourself and what you like.”.

According to recent reports, what does this mean for the rest of Jefferson’s NFL season? You can expect tons more tunnel-walk outfits, for starters. “Every week is another opportunity to bring something exciting to the tunnel,” he indicates. “We love finding ways to surprise people, turn heads, and keep things interesting.” Start taking your bets—fashion bets, not sporting bets—on what runway outfit or custom creation he will don next. “We’ve already had a few outfits this season that have gotten a lot of attention, and that’s always fun to see,” he says. “But for me, it’s not just about getting people talking—it’s about continuing to discover upcoming brands, experimenting with different styles, and finding creative ways to express myself through fashion.”.

  • One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.
  • Sources indicate that the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

Sources indicate that the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

Sources indicate that yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

Industry observers note that this is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls.

Whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Industry observers note that add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Recent findings suggest that add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

In a recent development, while the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

According to recent reports, butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

Industry observers note that “The first rule of acting is that you don’t judge your character,” Julia Garner told an enthralled audience on Thursday evening at Manhattan’s Paris Theater, moments after the credits rolled following the world premiere of The Altruists. The Netflix original series, available on the streaming platform now, sees Garner step into the shoes of Caroline Ellison, the disgraced co-CEO of Alameda Research and on-again, off-again girlfriend of FTX co-founder Sam Bankman-Fried. “I wasn’t necessarily thinking of the fraud. I just wanted people to be able to understand her,” she added.

In a recent development, after a screening of the surprisingly humorous pilot episode, Garner and her co-star, Anthony Boyle, joined the show’s creator, Graham Moore, for a panel discussion with actor-turned-journalist Ben McKenzie about the treachery, trickery, and turbulence that pervade the world of cryptocurrency. “You’re probably wondering what’s Ryan Atwood doing up here,” McKenzie joked from the stage, referring to his early-aughts turn as one of The O.C.’s leading teen heartthrobs. “For the last four years, I’ve been investigating and documenting fraud and other criminal activity… And having met and interviewed the real Sam Bankman-Fried, I would like to say that Anthony has a lot more charm [than him].”.

Sources indicate that the series doesn’t just chronicle the shocking fall of Bankman-Fried and FTX. Rather, it centers largely on the romantic trajectory of the two financial-industry protégés. “It’s the story of two people who I genuinely, to the core of my being, believe got into this for the right reasons and wanted to do the right thing,” Moore remarked. “But over the course of their tortuous relationship and those six years, they turned each other into people who did the exact opposite of the thing they initially set out to do.” (Drawing a laugh from the crowd, Northern Irish actor Boyle likened their dynamic to “something from an episode of Love on the Spectrum.”).

After the panel, Garner, in a custom ballet-slipper-pink jumpsuit by Haider Ackermann for Tom Ford and an earful of Lorraine Schwartz bling, and an all-black-clad Boyle joined their castmates, crew members, and press for an after-party in The Plaza Hotel’s Oak Room—making it one of the last industry events to be hosted in the storied venue before it closes for a four-year renovation.

Over mini-umbrella-adorned mai-tais and passed bites, guests discussed the show and compared notes on how much they actually understood crypto terminology, while twirling SBF-approved fidget spinners and branded poker chips around in their hands.

In a recent development, this flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

It has been revealed that you’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

Sources indicate that true to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

In a recent development, I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

In a recent development, this is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table rapidly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

Experts on How to Brighten Under Eyes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that without fail, the eyes are usually the first place a busy week (or month) demonstrates up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that without fail, the eyes are usually the first place a busy week (or month) demonstrates up. A late night, skipping your skin-care routine, or long flight easily translates to a little puffiness in the morning or some shadowing underneath, and maybe even the dreaded “eye bag.” It happens to everyone, and it usually fades once you’ve caught up on sleep, gotten back on your regimen, and have hydrated enough.

Some of it comes down to how the area is built. The skin around the eyes is thinner than on the rest of the face, so whatever’s going on underneath, like fluid that settled overnight or tiny blood vessels close to the surface, is easier to see. Over time, collagen gradually decreases and the brows can sit a touch lower, which is a completely normal part of getting older. Still, it’s nice to have a few tricks for the days you want to look as awake as you feel.

Recent findings suggest that the good news? There are plenty of ways we can brighten, lift, and hydrate this area of the face. Some are as easy as curling your lashes or keeping a couple of spoons in the freezer. Other methods, like an eye cream with studied ingredients, work slowly over a few months after a little consistency. If you want to go further, in-office treatments can subtly lift the brow or soften dark circles. Below, our experts share their best tips for brightening and lifting the eye area, starting with the simplest.

It has been revealed that makeup artist Lynsey Alexander has transformed many a tired eye in her time, having worked with models backstage at fashion highlights and on shoots for years. She always begins with good eye drops. “I then use a beige pencil secretly inside the eyes–it needs to be a skin-toned color, white is too stark,” she claims. “My favorite is from Paris Berlin as it’s quite dry and not overly creamy, something you don’t want as it moves too easily.”.

“Dark circles are a common complaint in my office,” notes aesthetic doctor, Maryam Zamani, MD. “One of the most common reasons for dark circles is loss of volume in the periorbital area. As we age, the eyelid-cheek junction becomes elongated, and where this junction was once confluent in youth, it becomes demarcated, giving the appearance of dark lower eyelids or tear troughs.” It’s a common problem that can begin from as early as your twenties, and is made worse as collagen stores deplete. Dr. Zamani often treats it with “meticulously placed micro-droplets of hyaluronic acid” to restore the lost volume and hydrate. You will see brighter, more awake eyes immediately.

Industry observers note that celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips has prepped clients like Hailey Bieber and Kendall Jenner for years, and she knows tired eyes are usually the first thing to give a face away. Her fix starts with a step she has coined called underglazing. “The under-eye area is one of the first places I focus on when prepping the skin because it’s so delicate, and can show dryness and fine lines more easily,” she indicates. “‘Underglazing’ is really about giving that area the hydration it needs before applying any makeup. I love using lightweight, hydrating skin care and gently pressing it into the skin to help everything absorb. The goal is to make the skin look naturally plump and hydrated, so you need less makeup to begin with.”.

It has been revealed that the fresh wave of the best eye creams are more effective than ever before, and come loaded with efficacious active ingredients to illuminate the area and soften fine lines, while maintaining the integrity of the skin barrier. “Tretinoin has the best evidence behind it–with continued use (for about a year), you see increased cell turnover; cue brightening of the skin and a reduction in wrinkles,” explains dermatologist Emma Craythorne, MD. “Azelaic acid is also brilliant at brightening, if used in strength at five per cent.”.

It has been revealed that if your glitch is puffiness, take care to ensure you opt for a detoxifying eye cream instead of a hydrating formula–according to Dr. Zamani, hydrating eye creams (particularly those with hyaluronic acid) may exacerbate it.

Yes, it’s boring, but what you eat and drink does make a big difference to the eye area. Those who have ever woken up the morning after with eyes that feel like lead will know that. “Keeping salt and alcohol low in your diet is key,” claims Dr, Zamani. “And sleeping with a pillow and eye mask can also help.”.

To stimulate the area and help de-puff, facialist Nichola Joss recommends gently massaging an eye cream or gel around the outer orbital bone. “You can also use cold teaspoons to gently stimulate, de-puff, improve lymph drainage and brighten the area,” she says. For those more serious about texture and pigmentation, she also recommends the Lyma Laser, which can be used at home.

Sources indicate that turns out there are a lot of veins and capillaries underneath delicate, thin skin in the eye area, which can cause the dark hue we recognize as dark circles. “We can use sophisticated lasers to target the vascular plexus in the upper and lower eyelid,” says aesthetic surgeon, Costas Papageorgiou, MD, who works from Harrods Wellness Clinic in London. “This plexus tends to become more prominent with age as a result of accumulative inflammation and loss of elasticity, to name two.” By addressing (and softening) this area, you can reinstate skin clarity and light reflection–plus it works particularly well when combined with under eye filler.

According to recent reports, to address cool tones and general darkness in the area, try color correcting. “For blue undertones, opt for a peach-based concealer,” advises Dr. Alexander, who also adds a touch of YSL’s cult Touche Eclat to reflect light in the area. “Then, set the under eyes with a brightening powder, such as Laura Mercier’s Secret Brightening Powder, for added radiance.”.

Simple but effective, curling your eyelashes has an immediate refreshing effect. “Creating a bright, lifted eye is about creating space between the brow and lash line, and drawing attention outwards and upwards,” explains Anna Payne, UK Chanel makeup artist. For a little extra oomph, she suggests applying a dot of highlighting shadow on the centre of the eyelid and inner corner of the eye to create an illuminating spotlight effect.

When we analyze drooping or lackluster eyes, we don’t often consider that part of the problem might be coming from the forehead. “One of the biggest reasons that the eye area looks tired is that on top of the tiny repetitive blinking movements our eyes have to do each day, we also express an array of emotions through them, too,” says Ada Ooi, TCM practitioner and founder of 001 Skincare. “A lot of our eye movements, such as frowning or surprise, come from muscles in the forehead.” She recommends using a gua sha tool to alleviate the tension built in the frontalis muscles (the vertical muscles that lift the brows). Try cross-friction massage (horizontally, in this case) to break them from their usual position, and release fascia stress.

Industry observers note that “Freshly threaded brows have transformational powers,” sys Vanita Parti MBE, founder of Blink Brow Bar. “By de-fluffing, removing excess stragglers and creating two neat, symmetrical brows, you open up the eyes immediately.” Lifting the arch also lifts and sculpts the entire face, so post-thread, seek to define them with a brow pencil or pomade.

If curling your lashes is already part of your morning, think of this as the version that lasts. Lash lift technician and founder of beauty studio Studio.Lbb recommends it to anyone who’d rather skip the curler altogether. “A lash lift enhances your natural lashes by lifting, curling and tinting them for a longer, darker and more defined look—without extensions or mascara,” she says. Results usually last six to eight weeks, so it’s a smart one to book before a vacation or a stretch of early mornings.

Sources indicate that for a quick lift without needles, celebrity facialist and founder of M.A.S.C. Studio Alessandro Cirino points to microcurrent, which sends low-level electrical currents through the skin to wake up the muscles underneath. “Microcurrent can help tone and firm the eye contour, for a fresher-looking result,” he adds. As for a permanent result, Cirino notes the research is still limited. Think of it more as a refresh before a massive day unless you keep up with a daily routine.

In a recent development, most people think of crow’s feet when it comes to injectables around the eyes, but the brow is the less obvious spot for injection. “When strategically placed, neuromodulators can subtly elevate the outer brow by relaxing the muscles responsible for pulling it downward,” claims Dr. Casey Goodman, medical director of TIEV. “In the right patient, even a slight elevation can make the eyes appear more open, rested, and refreshed.” Dosing matters more here than almost anywhere else on the face. “Overcorrecting can compromise natural expression or even create heaviness where we intended to create lift,” Goodman says. “The goal isn’t to make someone look treated. It’s to make them look like themselves, without the subtle signs of fatigue that may not reflect how they actually feel.”.

Recent findings suggest that when we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue's vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry's standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

Recent findings suggest that as it relates to brightening and lifting treatments, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: modality, ingredients, texture, packaging, finish, and the skin-care concerns they address. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before. Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving Eve BOGO deal, giving you a perfectly good excuse to grab a burrito with an old friend before the turkey, stuffing, and inevitable food coma take over.

The deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m. local time at participating U.S. restaurants, with the usual buy one entrée, get one free format we all know and love.

It has been revealed that but, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line. You’ll need to be a Chipotle Rewards member, order at the restaurant, and scan your Rewards card at checkout. The free entrée must cost the same as or less than the one you're buying, and you can claim up to five free entrées per check. Kids’ meals don't qualify, and ordering ahead through the app, online, or for delivery won't work.

The timing has changed a bit from last year, too, when it ran from 4 p.m. all the way until closing. This time, you've got a four-hour window, so make sure that one friend you have who’s perpetually late gets the memo.

In a recent development, “The response last year revealed us how much our guests embraced the occasion,” Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle's senior vice president of brand marketing, said in a statement. According to the chain, the promotion ended up being its biggest sales-driving campaign of 2025, so a return trip was probably inevitable.

And if you’re stuffed and don’t feel like leaving the couch the next day, there’s a little something for the post-Thanksgiving crowd as well. From Friday, November 27, through Monday, November 30, Chipotle is waiving its delivery fee on eligible orders placed through its app or website with code CYBER26. You’ll need to spend at least $10 in the U.S. or $12 in Canada, and delivery menu prices may be higher, with other fees still applying.

If nothing else, it’s a convenient excuse to take a break from the annual challenge of finding increasingly creative ways to eat leftover turkey.

Latest Update: HexClad Bakeware Review: This Set Is So Sturdy and Nonstick, I’m Ditching Parchment Paper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As an avid baker, I've been waiting for such a sturdy set.
  • Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
  • Industry observers note that serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

As an avid baker, I've been waiting for such a sturdy set.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Industry observers note that serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set. It's also gloriously nonstick.

In a recent development, when I got married a few years ago, I put a cohesive bakeware set on my registry to replace years of mismatched Goodwill finds. While it worked well for a few months, within a year it began to show serious signs of wear and tear. Baked-on grease stains, rust spots and even warping had me in the market for a new bakeware set much sooner than I expected.

So, when I heard that my favorite cookware brand was releasing a bakeware set promising a sturdy, nonstick experience, I jumped at the chance to test it. Here’s everything you need to know about the latest HexClad bakeware line, including my honest thoughts after two months of testing.

HexClad’s new hybrid bakeware set features six core pieces:.

Industry observers note that it merges the benefits of stainless steel and nonstick into one easy-to-clean package. HexClad’s “hybrid technology” combines hexagonal steel peaks with nonstick valleys to improve heat circulation and release after baking. In other words, this bakeware browns your food evenly without it sticking to the pan.

Other features include ergonomic handles and a 2.5mm tri-ply construction to prevent warping. It’s also oven-safe up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit and dishwasher-safe. You can even use your favorite metal spatula or tongs without scratching the surface. And, like all HexClad cookware, it comes with a lifetime warranty against manufacturer’s defects.

Recent findings suggest that I’ll admit: I’m already a substantial fan of HexClad. I reach for the brand’s skillets and knives daily, and I’ve hoped for years that they would release a bakeware line.

So, when the offer to test the new set landed in my inbox, I couldn’t say no. But would it live up to the hype I’d built up in my head? I put all six pieces through the paces for two months to find out.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that like all HexClad products I’ve tried, the bakeware packaging experience is impeccable. The set arrived securely in one substantial box, separated with foam. Each piece was also wrapped in a protective dust bag, which is a nice touch.

Immediately, I was awed by the construction of these pans. Just by touch, I could tell they were high quality. I grabbed my food scale to compare the weight of the HexClad pans to my go-to carbon steel pans. The HexClad options weighed more than twice as much as my existing bakeware. Talk about heft!

Now, some folks might not appreciate that extra weight—especially since the pans get even heavier when full of food. But as someone who often replaces her bakeware every few years due to warping or rusting, I’m excited for a sturdier option. I hope this is the last set of bakeware I ever need to order.

As a final step, I washed each piece and got ready to bake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

One of my favorite things to make with sourdough discard is a big loaf of focaccia bread, so that was a natural first test in the 13×9 HexClad pan. Focaccia dough is sticky, but a generous coating of olive oil helps prevent it from gluing to the pan. Still, after proofing and baking my bread as usual, I was impressed that the final product pulled slightly away from the pan’s edges, making it slide out with complete ease. The bottom and edges got nice and toasty brown, too.

A few nights later, I used the same focaccia dough to make a focaccia pizza. Same sticky dough, made even stickier with tomato sauce, cheese and toppings. Plus, since it’s such a rich dish, I cut back on the amount of olive oil I used. Despite all the add-ons, this focaccia baked and released from the pan just as beautifully as the first loaf.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

Next, I made a chocolate layer cake with the 9-inch round cake pans. Now, I’m typically a ride-or-die parchment paper user. I find cutting out perfectly sized parchment circles a tedious task, but it’s worthwhile insurance against my cakes sticking. But to truly put the HexClad pans’ nonstick properties to the test, I skipped adding parchment and simply greased my pans with a little butter and flour.

It has been revealed that after baking and 10 minutes of cooling came the moment of truth: Would it stick? Luckily, no! Both cakes released with minimal effort. I simply ran a butter knife around the rim of the cake before using the cooling rack to flip ’em out. It’s a good thing, too, because this was my dad’s birthday cake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

My nonstick tests continued with the 8×8 square pan when I whipped up a batch of candy bar blondies. These blondies used an assortment of leftover Halloween candy, so I thought for sure the caramel ooze from a Baby Ruth bar would cause some problems. But nope! Even without parchment paper, treats slipped right out of the pan.

But how does HexClad bakeware perform with healthier treats? For one final test, I baked a completely made-up “brownie” recipe with pumpkin seed butter, applesauce, molasses and cocoa. It was a gooey, chocolaty mess by the time I put it in the pan, yet it baked and released beautifully.

Finally, I put the baking sheet to the test.

Now, I already own the HexClad pizza steel, which I use almost daily. It’s my go-to for everything from frozen pizza to galettes to roasted broccoli, and I find that it works even better than an air fryer to yield crisp, golden brown bakes. I’ve remarked on many occasions that it’s my all-time favorite piece of bakeware, especially for savory foods.

Industry observers note that both the pizza steel and baking sheet utilize HexClad’s tri-ply construction with an aluminum core and TerraBond nonstick coating. The former is a jet black colorway, while the baking sheet is gray.

Across the board, I found the baking sheet could handle every task I threw its way—including roasting a spaghetti squash. Oftentimes, I find myself scrubbing for what feels like days after roasting squash and scouring off that sticky, burnt-on residue. The HexClad pan cleaned with a simple swipe from a damp paper towel.

During testing, I found the bottoms and handles of the HexClad bakeware smudged a bit. After all, it is made of stainless steel. This didn’t bother me, and it was easy to clean by handwashing and drying it immediately. Over time, I may need to use a more abrasive regimen to clean stainless steel.

Sources indicate that while the HexClad pans are very sturdy, you should still let them fully cool before washing. Don’t throw a hot pan directly in the sink. The pans are also dishwasher-safe, though handwashing is recommended. (And honestly, so easy thanks to the nonstick coating.).

According to recent reports, across the board, I’m impressed with the new HexClad bakeware line. I hope we see even more pieces in the future, like a muffin tin and loaf pan. Only time will tell exactly how it holds up, but from what I’ve experienced so far, this set really is designed to last a lifetime. (And I’ll be continuing to long-term test the set, and enhancement this review accordingly.).

Ready to take your bakes to the next level? This all-in-one set is great for beginners and pros alike.

Industry observers note that you can shop the full 6-piece bakeware set on the HexClad website for $399. Select styles, like 2-pack sets of small and medium baking sheets, are also available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

It has been revealed that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just highlighted up with string beans.”.

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

"Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

Recent findings suggest that it makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

At least now I know that if I ever get invited to Thanksgiving at Ina’s, I'll gladly let her handle the wine—and I know to keep the marshmallow-topped yams at home.

#157539. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished.
  • The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder.
  • Industry observers note that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, notes of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

Industry observers note that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the fresh podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

It has been revealed that the Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Industry observers note that whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman claims. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

It has been revealed that at Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she notes.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up rapidly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

According to recent reports, alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Industry observers note that preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

In a recent development, while potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Industry observers note that mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined.
  • I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone.
  • Imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

Imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

“Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” says Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”.

The pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

It has been revealed that cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Grace Natoli Sheldon for Taste of Home.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

In a recent development, poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

If you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

If any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

In a recent development, if the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

In a recent development, you should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

According to recent reports, there’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.

The 7 Most Common Mistakes Home Cooks Make When Cooking Mashed Potatoes

  • Sources indicate that mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical.
  • Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Sources indicate that mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

Thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

It doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

According to recent reports, like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so key. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

In the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

It has been revealed that another important thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

Sources indicate that anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

Whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a major batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.

Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious.
  • In a recent development, for years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates.
  • Industry observers note that of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

In a recent development, for years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

Industry observers note that of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

Sources indicate that personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

According to recent reports, absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

The same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

Mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

Sources indicate that sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

It has been revealed that green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

Turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

Macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Industry observers note that alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

It has been revealed that nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

Industry observers note that I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and plan on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”.

Whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

Industry observers note that I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

It has been revealed that the first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

How about your latest kitchen adventure?

I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have massive ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

What’s your treat-yourself splurge?

My favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

What’s your most cherished cookbook?

Sources indicate that marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that revealed me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from Upcoming England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

Industry observers note that there was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

In a recent development, I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

It has been revealed that while my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was substantial sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

A great recipe deserves a great pan. From getting evenly baked cake layers to lifting brownies out in one piece, your bakeware can make a big difference.

According to recent reports, here at Taste of Home, we’ve explored everything from which type of bakeware is right for you to our favorite bakes to make and share. We’re always keeping an eye out for tools and tips that help you get the most out of your time in the kitchen.

One of the latest innovations catching our attention? Hybrid bakeware. Hybrid cookware has already made a name for itself, and now the concept is making its way into bakeware. This emerging category puts a fresh spin on traditional baking pans, combining some of the best features of different materials.

Sources indicate that so what exactly is hybrid bakeware, and is it worth the kitchen upgrade? Let’s take a closer look.

Traditional bakeware usually features one primary material, such as aluminum, stainless steel or glass. Hybrid bakeware, on the other hand, takes a different approach by pairing multiple materials together. For example, durable stainless steel pairs with an easy-release ceramic nonstick coating. You get the best of both worlds in one pan.

It has been revealed that stainless steel and ceramic nonstick make a pretty dynamic duo in baking. Stainless steel delivers durability and provides a sturdy baking surface, while nonstick helps prevent baked goods from sticking to the pan.

Sources indicate that hexClad brings these materials together in a distinctive way, and the magic is in the pattern. Each piece features a patented, laser-etched surface with raised hexagonal stainless steel peaks and recessed ceramic nonstick valleys. The stainless steel peaks lift baked goods slightly off the pan, allowing air to circulate underneath, while a ceramic nonstick coating helps food release more easily.

Hybrid bakeware can make everyday baking easier, from achieving consistent oven results to releasing delicate treats without damage. “Those everyday details matter to me when I’m deciding what deserves space in my kitchen,” explains D’Aniello.
