📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite all the hype about a upcoming space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.

According to recent reports, but historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability. Such was the case five centuries ago, when most of Western Europe was agog over the importation of precious spices from East Asia.

The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.

For centuries, camels had enabled trickles of spices such as cloves, nutmeg, and ginger to make their way into the kitchens of the high and mighty, be they landed gentry or royalty.

Cloves originally grew in the volcanic soils of only a handful of small islands in the northern Moluccas archipelago, author Lewis Dartnell notes in his 2019 book âOrigins: How the Earth Shaped Human History.â And the nutmeg tree appeared on only nine pinprick-sized islands --- the Bandas-further south, Dartnell writes.

Recent findings suggest that dried nutmeg. Credit: Wikipedia.

According to recent reports, but as early as the late 15th century and the Age of Columbus, middlemen had run up the cost of these rare spices to such a degree that Portugal and Spain, in particular, were in competition for a sea route to the Moluccas. That is, the Moluccan archipelago in what is now Indonesia.

The idea was to travel point to point by sea and weed out a multitude of middlemen along the long Silk Road --- mostly stretching overland from the Black Sea and Mediterranean through northern India to China.

Thus, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan had a novel idea.

Magellan, born into a family of minor nobility and modest possessions, had somehow convinced Spainâs King Charles V that it was possible to reach the eastern riches by traveling west, author Romeu Gaspar writes in his 2026 book âThe Revolution of Magellan: How 500-Year-Old Rocket Science Changed the World.â.

Recent findings suggest that and even though Magellan tragically lost his life en route at least a remainder of his crew did circumnavigate the globe. In the process, they forever changed the course of history, commerce, and human exploration.

Dried spices were a lightweight, high-value, reasonably imperishable product with which to stuff a ship's hold on long voyages, John Keay writes in his 2005 book âThe Spice Route: A History.â The profits were huge; in 1515, the return on such cargo docked at Lisbon was 700 per cent, Keay notes.

By 1520, the income from Portugalâs spice trade provided 40 percent of the Crownâs total revenue, Dartnell writes in his book. Spices eventually became so prized that in 1677, the Dutch swapped the island of Manhattan for the nutmeg-rich island of Run Palau, he notes.

According to recent reports, A 21st century analogy to such commercial exploration might be if by the end of this century, space entrepreneurs were able to extract and then process rare minerals from the Moon or Mars or even accessible Main Belt asteroids. And then in a cost-efficient manner, reap the profits by bringing them back to Earth. Or at least low-Earth orbit.

To that end, NASA Apollo 17 astronaut and geologist Harrison Jack Schmitt has long argued for Helium-3 mining on the Moon. But until someone fulfills the economics of making cislunar Space profitable human exploration of our solar system is likely to lag. That's because throughout history, scientific innovation usually goes hand in hand with someone's quest for a large profit margin.

Industry observers note that A durable commercial reason for people to work in space could give human space science the transportation and infrastructure it needs, Ret. U.S. Brigadier Gen. Pete Worden, an astrophysicist, chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email.

Within the next fifty years at least, the future of scientific space exploration is arguably best served by robotic means rather than astronauts.

Iâd rely heavily on robots for science and give commercial companies a larger role in developing and operating human spaceflight systems, Worden, who directed NASA Ames Research Center from 2006 to 2015, told me via email. NASA should return to its roots in the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) by emphasizing research and technology development that industry and scientists can build on, he notes.

Routine human sorties beyond low-earth orbit are key.

If commercial space transportation becomes routine, agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) could support research that uses it, Worden argues.

Meanwhile, we are left with space programs that for decades have been hampered by both politics and economics and as a result, have limped along in fits and starts.

Sources indicate that over the past 30 years, NASAâs looks for the Moon and Mars have had to survive changes in administrations, budgets, and priorities, claims Worden. When a program needs agreement from too many people, it becomes harder to take sensible risks, he says.

If humanity can ever succeed in making forays beyond low Earth orbit that are commercially viable in the same way the 16th Century spice trade was profitable, then this new ocean of space-time could be ours for the taking.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, mars Seed tackles plenty of in-situ resource utilization challenges all at once.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as we gear up to eventually land a human on Mars, more and more ideas are coming out about how to prepare for that. A recent one from Pioneer Labs, a research institute founded by bioengineer Erika DeBenedictis to develop biological technologies for space exploration, is now available on arXiv, without any intends to release it in a paid journal as part of the âOpen Scienceâ policy of The Astera Institute, who funded the research. It details âMars Seedâ - a newly introduced architecture that is self-contained and can produce a full 870 sq meters of pressurized habitat using nothing but Martian inputs within roughly every four Earth years.

In a recent development, mars Seed tackles plenty of in-situ resource utilization challenges all at once. One of the most notable is weight. According to the paper, the entire system weighs in at 20 metric tons - well below the threshold of Martian payloads for Starship or NASAâs proposed 25 ton Mars landers. And crucially, rather than relying on sugar or chemical inputs from Earth, the entire system wonât need any further input from our home planet once it is established on the Red one.

The plan starts off with a landing at a mid-latitude Martian site, with flat terrain and sub-surface water ice deposits. Immediately after landing, an autonomous rover sets about unloading the packageâs hardware and assembling a 40kW nuclear fission reactor modeled on the compact nuclear reactors NASA is already developing for Mars and Moon missions. About a month later, the reactor should be fully up and running, providing both electricity and âwasteâ heat that can be used to climate control a habitat.

According to recent reports, fraser interviews Dr. Congrui Jin about using bioreactors to grow Martian habitats.

Recent findings suggest that or in the case of this particular mission structure, to melt some ice. The system would put the heat from the nuclear reactor into a Rodriguez well - a type of ice-drilling technique that melts a pocket of underground ice and pumps the liquid water to the surface, which has already been proven in Antarctica.

Water is a crucial component in the entire systemâs operation. Once the first supply of it has been obtained from the âRodwellâ as itâs known, the system uses a scaled-up version of the urine-recycling system presently in place on the International Space Station (ISS) to recover around 90 percent of the water from each production batch of material.

But water isnât the only component input from Mars itself - another is dirt, or âregolithâ in the language of space exploration. The paper estimates the system will require around four tons of Martian soil deposited into its hoppers every day. This could be collected by autonomous mining machines, like NASAâs RASSOR. Approximately 800 kg of that dirt is then stirred into water-filled mixing tanks to dissolve out nutrients like phosphorus and nitrogen. But that still leaves the most deadly component of Martian soil - perchlorates.

Sources indicate that fraser interviews Dr. Michael Hecht, one of the main scientists behind the MOXIE experiment to create oxygen out of the atmosphere of Mars.

While these would kill a normal microorganism, Pioneer Labsâ speciality is designing biological systems for use in space exploration. So they simply evolved a hardy strain of the bacterium Cupriavidus necator, which they call sPL.001, which can thrive in the equivalent of a perchlorate-laced broth of Martian regolith simulant back on Earth. That bacterium is also the key engine in creating the bioplastics that are used to 3D print the radiation-shielded habitats.

According to recent reports, bacteria need food though, and shipping it from Earth would be prohibitively expensive. So thereâs one final input to the system from the Red Planet - its atmosphere. The first step in that process is an upgraded version of the MOXIE experiment that successfully highlighted an ability to split the carbon dioxide in Marsâ atmosphere into carbon monoxide and oxygen.

According to recent reports, typically, that system simply gets rid of the carbon monoxide to capture the oxygen for use in rocket fuel. But in Mars Seed, carbon monoxide is actually the prize. Using a technique inspired by an emerging field called âelectro-agriculture,â the system combines waste carbon monoxide gas with water to produce liquid acetic acid - the main ingredient in vinegar.

Fraser talks in detail about what we can find to live off of when we eventually do send humans to the Red Planet.

While a diet of straight vinegar might not sound appealing to a human, to a microbe it's nourishing enough. In four separate 1,000L fermentation tanks, the engineered microbes eat this vinegar, combined with oxygen, packing themselves with a bioplastic called polyhydroxybutyrate, with the polymer eventually making up 70% of their body weight. At that point, a high-speed centrifuge harvests the bacteria cells from the liquid broth, and the resulting paste is split into two separate assembly lines.

According to recent reports, half of the raw paste is mixed with Martian dirt and fed into a giant gantry 3D printer, which then extrudes a corrugated, arched outer protective shell. Rovers then work to pile around 2m of dirt onto the outer shell, creating a barrier to the cosmic rays and micrometeorites that plague the Martian surface.

The other half of the bacteria is subjected to a pressure bath of liquid carbon dioxide, again pulled straight from the atmosphere. This extracts the pure bioplastic, which is then melted and spun into an airtight, reinforced inner tent that is capable of holding a breathable atmosphere.

Sources indicate that interview with Dr. Erika DeBenedictis, the founder of Pioneer Labs. Credit - The New Biology YouTube Channel.

Industry observers note that so, in essence, this 20 ton system can be dropped on Mars, including a pair of helping rovers, and extract all of the necessary components to continually and consistently build atmosphere-tight, safe shelter for astronauts, at a rate of about 75 sq meters every 130 days. The paper notes that, comparing the system to directly launching 20 tons of pre-made plastic building materials from Earth, the break-even point of the stand-alone biofabrication facility is around 1,400 Martian days - which lines up nicely with the two orbital alignment cycles NASA is planning to utilize before sending human crews.

Recent findings suggest that the main difference is that the biofabrication facility never stops producing those safe habitats, which clearly is a major advantage. Despite its promise, though, there are still plenty of engineering challenges to overcome before this system will be anywhere near launch ready. But, when that time comes, it appears that we might be able to literally grow safe habitats out of Martian water, air, and soil. And that is something any future mission planner will be thrilled to have as an option.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What remains in the brain after a psychedelic wears off could matter for future medicines, as rat scans revealed distinct activity patterns a week after three different drugs were given.
  • Psychedelic drugs are attracting growing interest as possible treatments for depression, anxiety, and addiction.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Southern Denmark compared three psychedelic drugs, LSD, psilocybin, and the synthetic compound 2C-B, using brain scans in rats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What remains in the brain after a psychedelic wears off could matter for future medicines, as rat scans revealed distinct activity patterns a week after three different drugs were given.

Psychedelic drugs are attracting growing interest as possible treatments for depression, anxiety, and addiction. Yet newly introduced research suggests that drugs often grouped together under the same label may affect the brain in very different ways, potentially influencing how scientists investigate their medical uses.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Southern Denmark compared three psychedelic drugs, LSD, psilocybin, and the synthetic compound 2C-B, using brain scans in rats. They examined changes in brain activity while the drugs were active and again one week later, after their immediate effects had worn off.

Unlike earlier studies that largely examined one psychedelic at a time, the direct comparison revealed distinct patterns for each drug. Only a few changes were shared across all three.

Recent findings suggest that “Psychedelic drugs are often discussed as if they work in the same way. But when we look at the brain, the differences are clear. Each drug appears to affect its own networks, and that is new knowledge,” states Mikael Palner, Associate Professor at the Department of Clinical Research at the University of Southern Denmark and senior author of the study.

While the drugs were active, LSD and 2C-B produced the greatest number of changes in brain activity. The researchers also identified different patterns one week later, suggesting that the effects of these substances may extend beyond their immediate action in the brain.

It has been revealed that “What is interesting is that the differences do not only appear while the drugs are active. We can also see different traces in the brain afterwards. 2C-B mainly affected areas linked to reward, LSD affected areas linked to habits and motivation, while psilocybin stood out by primarily affecting areas involved in emotions,” says Frederik Gudmundsen, first author of the study.

Gudmundsen completed his PhD at the University of Southern Denmark and is now a postdoc at the Department of Clinical Medicine, Translational Neuropsychiatry Unit, Aarhus University.

These differences could help researchers investigate whether certain psychedelics are better suited to treating particular conditions. However, the brain activity patterns alone cannot establish which drug, if any, would be more effective for a specific disorder.

“If the drugs affect the brain differently, it is also possible that they may eventually prove better suited to different disorders. We do not know that yet, but our study provides a biological starting point for investigating it,” explains Palner.

Several psychedelic drugs are already being investigated in clinical trials for conditions including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and addiction. Understanding how individual substances affect different brain networks could eventually help scientists develop more targeted approaches to treatment.

In a recent development, for now, the findings remain limited to experiments in rats and do not show whether the drugs are effective in patients. Further research in humans will be needed to determine whether the same differences occur in the human brain and whether they can help guide future psychedelic treatments.

In a recent development, reference: “Serotonergic psychedelics induce distinct patterns of metabolic activity and covariance within biologically informed rat brain networks” by Frederik Gudmundsen, Julia Czurylo, Daniel R. Tech Report: LISA's Gravitational Wave Detections Could Reveal Exoplanets

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, is scheduled to be launched in 2035.
  • GWs are ripples in spacetime that are the signatures of mergers between massive objects, either compact binaries containing stellar mass black holes, white dwarfs, and neutron stars, or between supermassive black holes (SMBH).
  • By detecting GWs from SMBH mergers, scientists study how galaxies merged and grew so massive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, is scheduled to be launched in 2035. The ESA is still developing the mission, but it's basic design is established. It will feature three separate spacecraft flying in an equilateral triangle formation. They'll be connected by laser interfometry, and LISA will use that interferometry to detect gravitational waves (GW).

GWs are ripples in spacetime that are the signatures of mergers between massive objects, either compact binaries containing stellar mass black holes, white dwarfs, and neutron stars, or between supermassive black holes (SMBH). Astronomy is concerned with light in all its wavelengths, but gravitational waves open another window on the Universe.

By detecting GWs from SMBH mergers, scientists study how galaxies merged and grew so massive. GWs from mergers between compact binaries can act as distance markers, helping cosmologists measure the expansion of the Universe. And the Universe was opaque to light in its first 380,000 years, so that time period is behind a curtain. But that curtain of opacity can't stop gravitational waves, so they can potentially bring those crucial years of the Universe's evolution into view.

But now researchers are saying that LISA may also be able to detect exoplanets.

This artist's impression highlights gravitational waves from the merger of two compact objects. The presence of an exoplanet can leave a signature on these waves that LISA can detect. Image credit: NASA.

âThe most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,â remarked Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland and NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center. âIf an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way weâll be able to uncover.â.

Two new papers outline LISA's planet-detection potential, and McGrath is involved in both. He's the sole author of "Receiving Exoplanet Messages with Gravitational-wave Carriers: The Gravitational-wave Radial Velocity Method," published in The Astrophysical Journal. It explains how LISA could detect exoplanets.

"Gravitational-wave (GW) radial velocity (RV) may offer a upcoming method for detecting exoplanets, one that would primarily target planets orbiting GW-emitting, ultracompact, post-main-sequence stellar objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes," McGrath writes in the first paper.

In a recent development, the GWRV operates on the same principle as the RV exoplanet detection method does. In those instances, astronomers measure the tiny wobble a star experiences as an orbiting exoplanet tugs on it. Stars rotate, and the visible part of the star rotating toward the observer is blue-shifted, while the visible part of the star rotating away is red-shifted. The wobble creates doppler shifts in the red and blue light that astronomers measure with spectrographs.

Recent findings suggest that in GWRV, an orbiting exoplanet creates a wobble in the center of mass of a compact binary. That creates a detectable doppler shift in the gravitational waves instead of in starlight. The method is more sensitive to high-mass, long-period planets than traditional RV, which more readily detects massive planets on short-period orbits around lower-mass stars like M dwarfs.

In a recent development, if the method works, it has some advantages over other exoplanet detection methods. "For one, GW observatories have potentially much farther reach into the Milky Way and beyond, since the GW amplitude is inversely proportional to the source distance," explains McGrath. "They will also inherently be probing post-main-sequence stellar systems, where EM observatories simply have not found as many exoplanets.".

According to recent reports, exoplanets that go undetected in compact binaries can also cloud the GW signal. That can create misunderstandings as researchers try to understand and constrain the GWs. So detecting them also clarifies the GW signal from the compact binary.

This graphic shows how LISA works by detecting tiny changes in the distances between the spacecraft. Image Credit: By ESA / ATG Medialab, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/144582237 This graphic shows how LISA works by detecting tiny changes in the distances between the spacecraft. Image Credit: By ESA / ATG Medialab, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/144582237.

It has been revealed that this work is just an initial attempt to understand how it could all work. There's much more work to be done, as McGrath himself acknowledges. For one thing, the movement of LISA itself introduces some Doppler effect into the signal that has to be managed. Ground-based GW observatories don't move, and LISA will be the first one that does.

"Future, more complex and robust analyses will be needed to better understand the ability to detect exoplanets in GW signals," McGrath writes. "But hopefully this work can better shed light on the fundamental physics that can inform those studies.".

If LISA does detect a signal in a GW that indicates a possible exoplanet, it will only be a candidate. That signal will have to be confirmed, and that will require observations in the electromagnetic regime. That's the subject of a second paper.

In a recent development, mcGrath is also the lead author on another paper in the same journal that focuses on validating GW exoplanet candidates. It's titled "Multimessenger Exoplanets: Combining Infrared Excess and Astrometry with Gravitational-wave Detections of Double White Dwarf Exoplanets." It explains how the JWST can confirm GW exoplanet detections, possibly with help from Gaia or the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

According to recent reports, âBy themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency," said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the second paper. "Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal.â.

It has been revealed that LISA will see these as signals that bracket the primary GW signal from the DWD. These secondary signals are positioned in frequencies above and below the primary. So while the primary signal carries information about the DWD, the secondaries carry information about the exoplanet.

Sources indicate that every observatory, whether electromagnetic or gravitational, is built to detect signals at particular frequencies. LISA's frequency range means it will excel at detecting DWDs with short orbital periods. White dwarfs aren't rare, since they're the main evolutionary outcome for stars like the Sun, once they leave the main sequence. DWDs are rarer than single WDs, but astronomers still think that there are about 10 million DWDs with orbital periods of less than one hour in the Milky Way. Of those 10 million, researchers expect LISA to find about 10,000.

Sources indicate that astronomers think that LISA will find about 10,000 white dwarf doubles (DWDs) with short orbital periods. LISA should be able to detect exoplanets in DWDs, if they're there. Image Credit: Tod Strohmayer (GSFC), CXC, NASA, Illustration: Dana Berry (CXC).

Sources indicate that LISA should be able to find the bracketed signals that exoplanets on circumbinary orbits around DWDs display. They would be candidates at first, and if those signals can be confirmed, they would be the first of those exoplanet types to be found.

"This population is unique: no such planets are presently known around DWDs, and only a handful of circumbinary planets around main-sequence stars and planets orbiting white dwarfs (WDs) have been identified," the authors write. "Independent EM confirmation will be essential, especially for the first GW-detected exoplanets, to validate this method.".

Sources indicate that validation is critical, and it'll rely on electromagnetic confirmation. In their work, they use a representive known DWD (ZTF J2243+5242) to compute its detectability by LISA GWRV. "We then demonstrate two complementary EM techniquesâJWST infrared (IR) excess and Gaia or Habitable Worlds Observatory astrometryâthat could independently confirm a GW-detected planet in this fiducial system," the authors write.

An exoplanet orbiting a DWD produces more infrared than the stars themselves. The JWST is all about detecting infrared light, and it should have no problem detecting infrared excess out to a distance of about 500 light years. In their test case for a DWD at that distance, the JWST can detect an exoplanet with about five Jupiter masses, while LISA could detect one much smaller, with as little as 0.5 Jupiter masses, under perfect conditions.

âOnce LISA captures its first exoplanet detections, it will be critical for us to validate some of them,â mentioned Mary Anne Limbach, an assistant research scientist at the University of Michigan and a co-author on the confirmation paper. âThese joint detections will allow us to establish that the gravitational signals correspond to genuine planets rather than false positives.â.

The authors say we're about to enter a latest phase of exoplanet detections once LISA is operational. The JWST's initial planned mission was for 5 to 10 years, but it may last 20. If it does, then it will overlap with LISA for several years, and it can be used to validate LISA exoplanet detections.

"A multimessenger exoplanet would be a historic discovery, and a DWD circumbinary would help to provide key insights into planetary and stellar evolution and into a part of the exoplanet census not yet probed," the authors write.

In a recent development, when the first gravitational wave was directly detected by LIGO/VIRGO in 2015, astronomers declared that a fresh window into the cosmos had been opened. LISA is prying that window open wider than ever, and as this work reveals, the view might be even more detailed than thought. If it can detect exoplanets beyond the scope of traditional methods, then it'll give astronomers an even more expansive view of the cosmos than they anticipated.

A Single Fluorescent Dye Can Now Reveal 14 Different Structures Inside Living Cells

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (479 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Peking University have developed a fluorescent dye that can distinguish at least 14 membrane-bound structures in living cells using subtle differences in their chemical environments.
  • It has been revealed that watching the inner workings of living cells has long been difficult because most fluorescent dyes highlight only one cellular structure at a time.
  • In a recent development, the dye changes color depending on the chemical environment surrounding it, allowing scientists to identify cellular structures without labeling each one separately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Peking University have developed a fluorescent dye that can distinguish at least 14 membrane-bound structures in living cells using subtle differences in their chemical environments.

It has been revealed that watching the inner workings of living cells has long been difficult because most fluorescent dyes highlight only one cellular structure at a time. Now, researchers at Peking University have developed a dye called JONR that can distinguish at least 14 different structures using a single stain.

In a recent development, the dye changes color depending on the chemical environment surrounding it, allowing scientists to identify cellular structures without labeling each one separately. In laboratory tests, JONR identified organelles with three times the accuracy of Nile red, a fluorescent dye that has been used for more than a century.

JONR is based on Nile red, which glows differently depending on its surroundings. It produces greener light in oily environments and redder light in more polar ones. However, Nile red’s limited color changes make it difficult to tell similar cell membranes apart.

It has been revealed that by modifying the dye’s molecular structure, the researchers increased its sensitivity to subtle differences between membranes. JONR also produces very little light in water, reducing unwanted background signals and making cellular structures easier to observe.

According to recent reports, using JONR, scientists were able to track interactions between structures inside living cells. They observed moving compartments called late endosomes pulling thin tubes of the endoplasmic reticulum, a network involved in processing proteins and other cellular activities.

It has been revealed that the dye also revealed differences in how tightly molecules are packed within membranes. With specialized microscopy, researchers could examine both membrane composition and molecular organization using the same stain.

Experiments involving nerve cells highlighted that JONR could detect how molecules are arranged along nerve fibers. Additional tests in migrating cells revealed differences between the membranes of structures involved in cell movement.

Sources indicate that the dye revealed no significant toxicity in cultured cells, but the research has not yet demonstrated its performance in living animals or humans. Some measurements also require specialized microscopes.

Although further testing is needed, JONR could allow researchers to study several cellular structures and their interactions without relying on multiple fluorescent dyes.

Reference: “Far-red-emitting Nile red with boosted solvatochromism enables multidimensional imaging of membrane heterogeneity and dynamics” by Mingqiao Liu, Yunzhe Fu, Xiaopeng Li, Haolin Zhang, Yumiao Ma, Meiqi Li, Chunyan Shan, Hongxi Zheng, Xiaoyi Lu, Yan Zhang, Li Yu, Peng Xi and Zhixing Chen, 23 February 2026, The Innovation. DOI: 10.1016/j.xinn.2026.101319.

Funding: Natural Science Foundation of Shandong Province (Major Basic Research Project), National Key Research and Development Program of China, Beijing Municipal Science and Technology Commission, Beijing National Laboratory for Molecular Sciences, National Natural Science Foundation of China.

NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this Wednesday (Nov.
  • It has been revealed that while we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
  • According to recent reports, one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a upcoming milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

It has been revealed that while we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

According to recent reports, one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

It has been revealed that voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Recent findings suggest that voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which introduced half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

It has been revealed that just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

It has been revealed that taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

According to recent reports, voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight.
  • That technology is liquid crystals, most commonly used in liquid crystal displays (LCDs).
  • This solution offers several advantages over traditional solar sails.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum, and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind âsolar sailingâ, which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed actually feasible. Now a newly introduced paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), has unveiled a clever technique that will allow these giant sails to steer sideways using a technology more commonly associated with flat-screen displays.

That technology is liquid crystals, most commonly used in liquid crystal displays (LCDs). Instead of having the sail itself act like a giant mirror and requiring it to angle itself in order to turn relative to the Sun, the sail described by the RIT researchers bends sunlight at a steep angle via diffraction, allowing the spacecraft to steer sideways while still facing directly at the Sun.

This solution offers several advantages over traditional solar sails. The best analogy to describe how is to think of holding an umbrella against a stiff breeze. If you hold the umbrella directly facing the direction of the wind, it will push you straight back â simple enough. But, if you want to âturnâ compared to the direction of the wind, you have to angle the umbrella. In so doing, you not only lower the total amount of wind hitting the umbrella, but also make it much harder to control.

Fraser talks about how critical folding of solar sails is to their operation.

In a recent development, traditional solar sails face the exact same problem, only in space instead of in an atmosphere and with sunlight instead of wind. Nearly a decade ago, Grover Swartzlander Jr, one of the paperâs authors and a professor at RIT, realized that microscopic optical patterns that reflected light to the side would replace mechanical tilting in solar sails. To prove his point, he received backing from NASAâs Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) program, and laid out the groundwork for what became diffractive solar sails.

When light hits a diffraction grating, the technical term for the microscopic patterns embedded in the sail similar to what is etched onto a CD, it bounces off at steep, predictable angles even when the surface is facing the Sun head-on. Pushing the light to one side provides the sail with an equal and opposite kick in the other direction, steering the spacecraft using nothing more than a simple roll.

Industry observers note that while much of the early work on diffractive sail prototypes focused on patterns etched into metal-coated films, they struggled with scaling and had a hard time rolling into a rocket fairing. Hence the turn to LCDs. The latest study, where the RIT team -drawing on technical input from BEAM engineering and diffractive-sail researchers at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.

Fraser talks about how great solar sails are for travel in the solar system and beyond.

In a recent development, these flexible plastics contain rod-shaped molecules that naturally twist into microscopic spirals, creating layers of differing refractive indices that bend light using a phenomenon called the Pancharatnam phase. This is a way of bending or delaying light by twisting the direction the waves wiggle (its âpolarizationâ). Sails made out of this material have the added advantage of being lightweight, flexible, and easy to scale up manufacturing while still being able to fit inside a compact spacecraft.

Industry observers note that thereâs only one problem - a single liquid crystal layer only interacts with a very specific wavelength of light, allowing the rest to pass through unimpeded, and taking all their pushing power with them. To figure out how to solve this problem, the researchers turned to computer simulations, eventually using an optimization algorithm to design a three-layer sandwich of liquid crystals. The top layer catches blue and visible light, the middle layer grabs infrared, and the bottom layer interacts only with longer infrared rays. Even with those three separate layers, the combined film is only 5.5 micrometers thick, one-tenth the width of a human hair.

According to recent reports, such a setup would offer a major advantage in one potential use for a massive solar sail - as a âplanetary sunshadeâ. Scientists have long proposed parking a giant sheet in orbit at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point to deflect a small fraction of the sunlight reaching the planet, in an effort to intentionally cool it. With traditional materials, such a shade would need to tilt in order to keep its position, consequently shrinking its shadow. But one made out of diffractive material could hold its position without compromising its size. And with the new chiral liquid crystal setup, if the middle layer is left out, the near-infrared wavelengths used by solar panels to generate electricity would still pass through - or the layers could be tuned to let the red light needed for plant photosynthesis pass through - while the rest of the sunlight still pushes on the sail.

Fraser talks about what a solar sail actually is.

According to recent reports, all that being said, this concept is still at a very early stage. They havenât yet built a prototype of the three-layer system, let alone one that could stand the rigors of launch or the constant bombardment of the solar wind. But the paper offers a step to a potential solution to one of the most fundamental problems in solar sail design - and given the major advantages it has as a propulsion system, itâs only a matter of time before someone trials this new idea in the vacuum of space.

A Tiny Twist Reveals a Hidden Atomic Grid That Changes How Electricity Behaves

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets creates a hidden grid of atomic defects that alters how electrical charges are distributed.
  • It has been revealed that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets together has allowed scientists to create a hidden grid of atomic defects that influences how electrical charges are arranged.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery, led by researchers at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and published in Nature, demonstrates how the angle between two bonded crystals can control the spacing of defects at their interface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets creates a hidden grid of atomic defects that alters how electrical charges are distributed.

It has been revealed that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets together has allowed scientists to create a hidden grid of atomic defects that influences how electrical charges are arranged. The grid forms where the crystals meet, producing tiny patterns of electrical polarization that could eventually help researchers develop new electronic technologies.

According to recent reports, the discovery, led by researchers at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and published in Nature, demonstrates how the angle between two bonded crystals can control the spacing of defects at their interface. Although practical applications remain uncertain, the technique offers a way to engineer electrical structures at the nanoscale.

In a recent development, the researchers worked with strontium titanate (SrTiO3), a chemically stable oxide widely studied for its electronic properties. They fabricated crystal sheets just 10 nanometers (about 0.0000004 inches) thick and assembled them with a controlled twist.

Recent findings suggest that the underlying principle resembles a moiré pattern, which appears when two regular grids overlap at slightly different angles. However, strong bonding between the crystal sheets caused their atoms to rearrange at the interface. The remaining mismatch became concentrated along narrow regions of crystal distortion called dislocations, forming a repeating square grid.

Sources indicate that “We have spent years learning how to make high-quality sheets, put them together in the right position, bond them and twist them. Once you can do all of that, you can start looking at what happens where these two sheets meet,” says Professor Nini Pryds of DTU.

“So, the bonding is essential to understanding what happens between the layers.”.

The grid was first predicted by William Sandholt, then a Ph.D. student at DTU, using machine learning simulations to calculate how atoms would rearrange as the crystals bonded and twisted. His results identified a network of dislocations that the researchers subsequently searched for experimentally.

Industry observers note that early electron microscope images showed what appeared to be an ordinary moiré pattern, with no obvious sign of the predicted defects. One difficulty was that the microscope’s electron beam passed through material on both sides of the buried interface, making its atomic structure difficult to isolate.

“The electron beam goes through about ten nanometers of material, reaches the interface, and then goes through another ten nanometers. So, the image is influenced by the material on both sides of what we want to see,” explains John Mangeri, a postdoc at DTU and joint first author of the study.

To overcome this problem, the team simulated how electrons traveled through the samples and examined thin cross sections cut in different directions. Electron microscopy performed with collaborators at the University of Antwerp in Belgium and the SuperSTEM Laboratory in the UK ultimately confirmed the predicted grid.

“Right where the sheets met, we could see the repeating pattern, and it agreed almost perfectly with the theory. That was amazing.”.

Pryds emphasizes that the theoretical predictions were essential to the discovery.

It has been revealed that “We would never have discovered the dislocations if the calculations had not predicted their existence. The finding highlights the power of combining theory and experiment, bringing together researchers who synthesized the ultrathin sheets, assembled them with a controlled twist, simulated their behavior, and examined the resulting material.”.

It has been revealed that further simulations showed that the atomic distortions surrounding the dislocations could slightly separate positive and negative electrical charges. This separation, known as polarization, formed swirling patterns around the grid. Additional microscopy, interpreted alongside the simulations, supported the connection between the atomic distortions and these electrical structures.

The spacing of the grid also depends on the angle between the crystal sheets, providing a means of adjusting the size of the resulting patterns.

Recent findings suggest that “Changing the twist angle changes the spacing between the dislocations. So now, we have a way to control how small the structure becomes,” indicates joint first author William Sandholt.

“These dislocations could be used for memory applications, for example, and the grid could be tuned through the twist angle.”.

Electrical polarization plays a role in technologies such as memory devices and energy storage systems, making these structures potential candidates for future research. The team plans to investigate whether the same approach can produce useful electrical behavior in strontium titanate or other oxides.

Industry observers note that reference: “Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites” by W. Sandholt, N. Gauquelin, J. Mangeri, A. Annys, J. M. Hansen, A. R. Insinga, E. Dollekamp, N. Vitaliti, G. Panchal, T. Chennit, A. De Backer, D. Kepaptsoglou, R. Mandal, D. R. Rodrigues, S. Van Aert, H. Nguyen, K. I. Wurster, A. Bhowmik, I. E. Castelli, S. B. Simonsen, T. S. Jespersen, Q. M. Ramasse, R. D. James, B. Jalan, J. Verbeeck, J. M. G. Lastra and N. Pryds, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11330-9.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. It has been revealed that sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

Detecting Primordial Black Holes By The Stars They Destroy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that dark matter is hypothetical matter that makes up the large majority of the matter in the Universe, but we can't see it because it doesn't interact with light.
  • Recent findings suggest that primordial black holes are hypothesized to have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, from the direct collapse of pockets of dense matter.
  • In a recent development, the research is "The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that dark matter is hypothetical matter that makes up the large majority of the matter in the Universe, but we can't see it because it doesn't interact with light. Scientists put their minds into hyperdrive trying to understand it and figure out what it is. One of the proposals is that primordial black holes (PBH) account for some or all of dark matter.

Recent findings suggest that primordial black holes are hypothesized to have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, from the direct collapse of pockets of dense matter. Really small PBHs wouldn't have survived this long because of Hawking Radiation, but more massive ones could have. Fresh research focuses on asteroid-mass PBHs and how they could be detected, if they exist.

In a recent development, the research is "The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The lead author is Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT. The authors focus on what are called Hawking stars, stars that have engulfed a microscopic PBH. They're named after renowned physicist Stephen Hawking, who first proposed them in the 1970s.

"Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window (1017â1023 g) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars," the authors write. Though it's all theoretical at this point, the researchers developed a framework for what would happen to stars that capture these PBH. They used stellar evolution models, simulations, and other tools to try to understand what would happen.

Primordial Black Holes are only theoretical, so far. But if they exist, they could find their way inside main sequence stars. Image Credit: NASA and G. Bacon/STSCI.

First of all, a single star on its own is unlikely to capture a PBH. But a star with a stellar or planetary companion would have enough gravitational interactions to trap a PBH in one of the stars. It could take thousands or even millions of year for a PBH to work its way into a star's center.

Industry observers note that âThen, this is where the action begins,â said lead author Gottlieb. Once the PBH reaches the center, the star can't survive.

It has been revealed that according to this work, there are two outcomes for stars that suffer this misfortune, and both spell doom. "We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly," the authors write.

Once a PBH finds its way into the center of a star, it takes only a few million years before it consumes about 1% of the star's mass. Then, the rotation rate comes into play. If it's fast enough, the star's gas can't fall directly into the PBH. Instead, an accretion disk forms around the PBH, inside the star. This is where the two outcomes diverge.

Recent findings suggest that âInside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,â Gottlieb stated. This is an almost unimaginable scenario, but the research demonstrates it's possible.

âThe black hole is also spinning, and itâs twisting space and time.â.

The PBH then warps the star's magnetic fields, and just like in a SMBH, powerful jets are rolled out. âThis twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,â Gottlieb explains.

What star could survive powerful jets being emitted from inside?

âOnce the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,â said lead author Gottlieb. The authors write that this produces "an explosive Hawking-star transient powered by a rapidly spinning PBH." The PBH emits jets that tear through the star, quickly destroying it.

Industry observers note that âAnd these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds," Gottlieb noted. "Itâs very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.â.

Sources indicate that this schematic illustration highlights the evolutionary sequence of a Hawking star. First the PBH is captured, and eventually it migrates into the stellar core. Once the PBH is embedded in the core, the PBH grows by accreting stellar mass. What happens next depends on whether the PBH forms a disk before it consumes its host. If a disk forms, that warps the magnetic fields, and the PBH releases jets from inside the star, destroying it in seconds. If no disk forms, the star dies a quiet, gradual death, and a stellar-mass black hole is left behind. Image Credit: Ore Gottlieb et al 2026 ApJ 1012 157.

Sources indicate that in the second case, the star's destruction is less cinematic. "The system dies quietly," the authors write, "leaving a PBH with mass of the order of the consumed stellar mass and little or no bright disk-powered emission." It's basically a stellar-mass black hole indistinguishable from others of its kind.

These two paths to destruction create different prospects for observing PBHs engulfed by stars.

According to recent reports, "Our results carry important observational implications across both electromagnetic and GW channels," the authors explain. "If a PBH has grown sufficiently to form an accretion disk, the associated disk winds and relativistic jets can inject enough energy and momentum into the stellar envelope to unbind the star and power an explosive transient.".

Sources indicate that the rapid destruction creates a bright transient that emits EM radation across multiple wavelengths. This could be detectable at long distances with modern telescopes, similar to supernovae.

âWe would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,â Gottlieb indicates. âThis is something we could potentially detect, if itâs not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.â.

Industry observers note that this simulation depicts the moments after a primordial black hole is captured by a star. As soon as the black hole falls into the starâs center, it creates a swirling disk of material (orange). Within a matter of seconds, interactions between the black hole and the spinning disk should launch powerful jets of matter that ultimately pierce through the star, making it explode.

Sources indicate that GWs from these events are likely more rare. Scientists have long wondered if PBH could be GW sources, and it's possible that the Hawking-star remnant that's left behind could be detected as one if it ever formed a compact binary with another compact object. The authors say that if this happens, it's exceedingly rare. But if it does happen, observing them would be very informative. "Thus, GW detections would be highly diagnostic if found, but should be regarded as a binary-evolution-limited and likely subdominant discovery channel for Hawking stars.

Here's where dark matter comes in. These Hawking-stars, if they exist and can be detected individually, could be used to calculate their population. If these stars work the way the researchers think they work, they can be detected and used to "provide independent observational constraints on the PBH population," the authors write. But on the other hand, "the absence of such transients or of convincing subsolar merger candidates could constrain the fraction of DM in PBHs.".

So it seems there's a potential viable pathway to detect dark matter, if indeed PBHs are real and astronomers can find them destroying a star in a telltale blinding flash.

It has been revealed that âThere is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,â Gottlieb noted. âWe expect this to be visible, and itâs something we should look into.â.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saharan dust helps nourish the Amazon, showing why scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look far beyond their own borders.
  • Nearly everything we eat depends on the thin layer of soil covering Earth’s surface.
  • Estimates cited in a study published in the European Journal of Soil Science suggest that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is already degraded, putting US$44 trillion in annual economic output at risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saharan dust helps nourish the Amazon, showing why scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look far beyond their own borders.

Nearly everything we eat depends on the thin layer of soil covering Earth’s surface. This vital resource also filters water, stores carbon, and supports ecosystems that sustain life. Yet despite its importance, soil remains without a dedicated international treaty to protect it.

Estimates cited in a study published in the European Journal of Soil Science suggest that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is already degraded, putting US$44 trillion in annual economic output at risk.

According to recent reports, binding international agreements protect the atmosphere, biodiversity, and the high seas. Soil, an estimated US$325 trillion (A$473 trillion) natural asset, receives fragmented protection through agreements on climate change, biodiversity, and desertification.

It has been revealed that the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification focuses on drylands, while other agreements address individual functions such as carbon storage or biodiversity. None provides comprehensive, binding protection for soil as a planetary system.

The paper’s authors, University of Sydney soil scientists Dr. Quentin Styc and Professor Alex McBratney, argue that this gap partly reflects a misunderstanding of the resource itself.

Recent findings suggest that “We have spent centuries classifying soils according to their different properties, uses and locations. But in doing so, we’ve lost sight of the bigger picture,” mentioned lead author Dr. Styc, from the university’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences and Sydney Institute of Agriculture.

In a recent development, consider the connection between the Sahara Desert and the Amazon rainforest. Each year, around 27.7 million metric tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic, delivering roughly 22,000 metric tons of phosphorus to the Amazon. This natural fertilization replaces nutrients lost through flooding, helping sustain one of the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems.

Erosion, pesticide contamination, and microplastics can also spread across borders, while soil degradation can contribute to climate change and food insecurity far from the affected region.

“Soil doesn’t stop functioning at national borders. What happens to soil in one country can have profound consequences for ecosystems, economies and food security on the other side of the world.

According to recent reports, “We have international treaties to protect the ocean and atmosphere. Yet the soil beneath our feet, which is fundamental to human civilization, remains without equivalent protection.”.

For Styc and McBratney, these links mean soil must be understood and protected as one interconnected global system.

“These connections demonstrate why soil security cannot be achieved by countries acting independently,” Dr. Styc noted.

Recent findings suggest that “We need to think about soil in the singular, just as we increasingly talk about one ocean rather than separate oceans. It’s a change in language that reflects a much bigger change in how we understand our responsibility for the planet.”.

A proposal for international protection is already taking shape. Aroura, a global soil security think tank established at the University of Sydney, has outlined an eight-stage pathway toward a Global Convention to Secure Soil, targeting adoption in 2032. The proposed convention would coordinate international efforts while allowing countries to develop strategies suited to their environmental and economic circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that in October 2025, the International Union for Conservation of Nature approved a resolution calling for a binding international legal instrument on soil security. Ocean governance offers a model for what cooperation could achieve. After decades of negotiations, an international agreement protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdictions entered into force in January 2026.

“When environmental damage crosses borders, international cooperation needs to match the scale of the problem. We cannot solve a planetary challenge with a patchwork of disconnected policies,” Dr. Styc mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that aroura brings together an international panel of leading experts in soil science, economics, law, and social science to develop the scientific evidence and policy frameworks needed for a convention. It hosted the Third Global Soil Security Summit at the University of Sydney from October 20 to 23, 2026.

“Soil underpins our food systems, biodiversity, water security and climate resilience, yet it remains largely invisible in international environmental governance,” remarked co-author Professor McBratney, a leading international soil scientist who was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that “Through Aroura, we are working to build the scientific and policy foundations for a global convention that recognizes soil as a shared responsibility. We have the knowledge and the tools. What we need now is international commitment.”.

According to recent reports, reference: “One Soil, One Planet, No Treaty” by Quentin Styc and Alex McBratney, 3 November 2026, European Journal of Soil Science. DOI: 10.1111/ejss.70448.
